source_text: Ἐκτίθεται δὲ μετὰ ταῦτα ὁ Κέλσου Ἰουδαῖος ὡς ἀκόλουθον τὸ μὴ ἀκόλουθον. οὐ γὰρ ἀκολουθεῖ τῷ ἠθέλησεν ἡμᾶς δι᾿ ὧν πέπονθε κολάσεων διδάξαι καὶ θανάτου καταφρονεῖν τὸ ἀναστάντα αὐτὸν ἐκ νεκρῶν φανερῶς εἰς φῶς καλέσαι πάντας καὶ διδάξαι, οὗ χάριν κατεληλύθει. εἰς φῶς γὰρ πρότερον ἐκάλεσε πάντας εἰπών· „δεῦτε πάντες οἱ κοπιῶντες καὶ πεφορτισμένοι, κἀγὼ ἀναπαύσω ὑμᾶς.“ καὶ οὗ χάριν κατελήλυθεν, ἀναγέγραπται ἐν οἷς ἀποτάδην κεκίνηκε λόγοις ἐν μακαρισμοῖς καὶ τοῖς ἑξῆς αὐτοῖς ἀπαγγελλομένοις καὶ ἐν παραβολαῖς καὶ ἐν ταῖς πρὸς τοὺς γραμματεῖς καὶ Φαρισαίους ὁμιλίαις. τὸ δὲ κατὰ Ἰωάννην εὐαγγέλιον ὅσα ἐδίδαξεν ἔκκειται, παριστάντα τὴν Ἰησοῦ οὐκ ἐν λέξεσιν ἀλλ᾿ ἐν πράγμασι μεγαλοφωνίαν· καὶ δῆλός ἐστιν ἐκ τῶν εὐαγγελίων ὅτι „ἐν ἐξουσίᾳ ἦν ὁ λόγος αὐτοῦ,“ ἐφ᾿ ᾧ καὶ ἐθαύμαζον.
pass_a_gloss: The Jew of Celsus sets out (ἐκτίθημι) after these things as consequent (ἀκόλουθον) the not-consequent. For it does not follow (ἀκολουθέω) upon the 'he wished (θέλω) to teach (διδάσκω) us through the punishments (κόλασις) which he suffered (πάσχω) to despise (καταφρονέω) also death (θάνατος)' that 'having risen from dead openly (φανερῶς) [he should] call (καλέω) all into light (φῶς) and teach for the sake of what (οὗ χάριν) he had come down (κατέρχομαι).' For he called all into light earlier (πρότερον), saying: 'Come (δεῦτε), all the laboring (κοπιάω) and burdened (φορτίζω), and I will give rest (ἀναπαύω) to you.' And for the sake of what he has come down is recorded in the words which he set in motion (κινέω) at length/extended (ἀποτάδην), in beatitudes (μακαρισμός) and the things announced next after them, and in parables (παραβολή), and in the conversations/discourses (ὁμιλία) toward the scribes (γραμματεύς) and Pharisees. And the according-to-John gospel: as many things as he taught are set out (ἔκκειμαι), presenting (παρίστημι) the grand-utterance (μεγαλοφωνία) of Jesus not in words/phrases (λέξις) but in realities/deeds (πρᾶγμα). And it is clear from the gospels that 'his word (λόγος) was in authority (ἐξουσία),' at which also they were marveling (θαυμάζω).
pass_b_english: After this Celsus’s Jew sets out as a consequence what does not follow. For from “He wished, by the punishments he suffered, to teach us to despise even death,” it does not follow that “after rising from the dead he should openly call all to the light and teach why he had come down.” For he had called all to the light earlier, saying, “Come, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

And why he had come down is recorded in the discourses he delivered at length: in the Beatitudes (Matthew 5:3–12) and in what is proclaimed after them, in parables, and in his conversations with the scribes and Pharisees. And in the Gospel according to John are set out the things he taught, which show the grandeur of Jesus’ speech, a grandeur not of phrasing but of substance. And it is clear from the Gospels that “his word was with authority” (Luke 4:32; compare Matthew 7:28–29), at which they marveled.

choices.why: Removed added 'them' from Celsus's 'teach why he had come down'

John clause: 'all that he taught is set out, and it shows' made 'are set out the things he taught, which show' (ὅσα; παριστάντα agrees with ὅσα, not with the Gospel; 'all' claimed a completeness the Greek does not)

anf_compare.notes: Crombie (ANF 1872) and Chadwick (1953) were not used or consulted; English is from the Greek.

Independent clause review: every clause checked; verdict pass.
Scripture citations sit inline beside the clause in Pass B.

translator_notes: Celsus’s two clauses are put in double quotation marks: the premise he grants (‘He wished... to teach us to despise even death’) and the conclusion he draws (‘after rising... he should openly call all to the light’). The ‘us’ is the Christians’ claim as Celsus’s Jew reports it; kept. καί before θανάτου is rendered ‘even death’. Matthew 11:28 is quoted without πρός με (‘to me’); rendered as Origen has it. ‘What is proclaimed after them’ refers to the rest of the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:13-7:27); only the Beatitudes are cited inline. The conversations with the scribes and Pharisees are too general for a single citation. In ‘And in the Gospel according to John...’, τὸ κατὰ Ἰωάννην εὐαγγέλιον stands without a construing verb and is taken as setting the frame; παριστάντα (neuter plural) agrees with ὅσα ἐδίδαξεν, so it is the things taught that show the grandeur (‘which show’). ὅσα is rendered ‘the things he taught’, not ‘all that he taught’, to avoid a claim of completeness the Greek does not make. μεγαλοφωνία (‘grandeur of speech’) with ‘not in words but in realities’ is rendered ‘not of phrasing but of substance’. ‘His word was with authority’ matches Luke 4:32 exactly.
